deep.reconstruction:
The page continues the previous one (folio 54r: x^7 - 28x^4 + 76.19031634 = 0, 'Zug II, 180°'). It treats three more members of the one-parameter family x^7 - 28x^4 + c = 0, now with complex constant c:
(A) c = 424.1152090 + 27.73434 i
(B) c = 135.8847910 + 27.73434 i
(C) c = 280 + 39.222279 i (marginal 'Zug II 90°')
For each equation Gauss lists all seven roots ('Wurzeln') x_k = a_k + b_k i to 7 decimals. He also gives each root in polar form x_k = ± r_k (cos S_k + i sin S_k), with 0 ≤ S_k < 180°. The column 'log r' is log10 r_k, and the suffix 'n' marks the minus sign, i.e. Re x_k < 0. Example: -1.8724430 - 0.0267580 i = -(1.87263)(cos 0°49'7.4'' + i sin 0°49'7.4''), and log10 1.87263 = 0.2724529.

Three control sums follow, which I take to be Gauss's checks on the computed roots:
(1) 'Summe' of the roots ≈ 0, because the x^6 coefficient is 0. The residuals are of order 1e-6.
(2) Σ log r_k = log f, where f = |c|, because ∏ x_k = (-1)^7 c = -c. Sums are 2.6284104, 2.1420331, 2.4513775 against 2.6284104, 2.1420333, 2.4513776.
(3) Σ S_k ≡ φ = arg c (mod 180°), where tan φ = Im c / Re c.

The sign bookkeeping works out exactly (my verification). In (A) there are four 'n' roots and ΣS = 543°44'29'' = 3·180° + φ. The product is therefore (+1)·|c|·e^{i(540°+φ)} = -c, as required. In (C), ΣS = 547°58' = 540° + 7°58'. In (B), ΣS = 371°32' = 2·180° + 11°32', again with four 'n' roots. Gauss records only ΣS mod 180°.

Computed checks (mine):
(A) |c| = 425.021, log10 = 2.62841; φ = atan(27.73434/424.1152) = 3.7414° = 3°44'29''.
(B) |c| = 138.686, log10 = 2.14203; φ = atan(0.204103) = 11°32'8''.
(C) |c| = 282.734, log10 = 2.45138; φ = atan(0.140079) = 7°58'27''.
Spot check of root (C7) ≈ 2.88398 - 0.02929 i by one Newton step from the real approximation (mine): x^7 - 28x^4 + 280 ≈ 2.3 at x = 2.884, and P'(x) ≈ 1341. The correction is -(2.3 + 39.22 i)/1341 ≈ -0.0017 - 0.0293 i, which matches the listed imaginary part.

Purpose: the labels 'Zug II 180°', 'Zug II 90°', 'Zug IV 90°' (next page, c = 280 + 651.52373 i) suggest a systematic tabulation of how the 7 roots move as c runs along certain paths ('Züge') in the c-plane. This is the root continuation along curves that underlies Gauss's geometric (1799/1849) treatment of the fundamental theorem of algebra. The precise meaning of 'Zug' and of the angle labels is not determinable from this page alone.

The critical values of c (double roots) are c = 0 and c = 192·16^{1/3}·ω ≈ 483.8·ω, with ω^3 = 1 (mine). The tabulated c lie away from these.
errors: No genuine errors found. Root sums deviate from 0 by at most ~1.6e-6, and log-sums differ from log|c| by 1-2 units in the 7th decimal; both are rounding effects.
Angle sums differ from arg c by ~0.01'' (e.g. 3°44'29.191'' vs 29.182''), which is rounding.
Angle sums are tacitly reduced mod 180°. This is consistent because the number of 'n' signs together with the multiple of 180° yields ∏x_k = -c. This is a convention, not a slip.
In the second 'Summe' line the imaginary part '-0,0000011' lacks the '.i'. This is an omission in the original.

results.what: Numerical computation of all seven complex roots of x^7 - 28x^4 + c = 0 for complex c, to 7 decimals, with polar form and logarithmic checks
results.modern_name: numerical polynomial root finding / root continuation (homotopy) in the parameter c
results.usually_credited_to: standard numerical practice; root-continuation ideas from 19th-century function theory (Puiseux, Riemann)

results.what: Checks via the Vieta relations: Σx_k = 0 and ∏x_k = -c, applied to the moduli (Σ log r_k = log|c|) and to the arguments (ΣS_k ≡ arg c mod 180°)
results.modern_name: Vieta's formulas used as computational checks

results.what: Tabulating root positions along paths ('Züge') in the parameter plane, presumably connected with the geometric proof of the fundamental theorem of algebra
results.modern_name: monodromy / continuation of algebraic roots along paths
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss's FTA proofs (1799, 1849) for the curve method; Puiseux (1850) for monodromy

deep.surprise_reason: This is a careful numerical table of roots with standard Vieta checks. It is impressive computational work, probably illustrating root curves related to Gauss's FTA work, but contains no new theoretical result.
